I'm not so sure about the anonymous box idea anymore. First of all, we'd then have to distribute the CSS properties on the FIELDSET node between the wrapper box and the contents container. Things like 'width', 'border', 'background' 'float', 'z-index', 'position' and 'transform' would intuitively belong in the wrapper, while 'display' and 'overflow' would have to be set on the contents container anonymous box. Do we want to go there?

WebKit creates just one box for a FIELDSET (box type determined by 'display'). The legend is simply encapsulated into the border block-start area. Any chance we could just spec it like that? Having the legend encapsulated into the border makes a lot of sense, e.g. when it comes to determining the containing block size for out-of-flow positioned descendants (in the cases where the FIELDSET isn't statically positioned). Scrolling would also work well then, since borders are outside the scrollport.

One thing that's still not obvious with this approach, though, is paint order. Should the legend be painted in the same phase as the borders (unless the legend establishes a stacking context entry (position:relative, etc.))?

Another thing would be that the used border-width may diverge from the computed border-width. Is that a problem?

The spec doesn't read that way to me:
> the border is expected to not be painted behind the rectangle at the rendered legend's static position (ignoring transforms on the rendered legend) with the same inline size as the rendered legend's border box and the same block size as the rendered legend's border box or the fieldset element's border width on the block start side, whichever is greater

The rectangle where the border shouldn't be painted will have its block size set to the border width, if it's larger than the legend's border box block size. There's something missing here, though, because if the border is larger than the legend, the block offset of the rectangle should be adjusted to the start of the border.

Painting the border around (on all four sides) of the legend if the legend is smaller than the border is certainly something that no browser does today (and, like I mentioned, not what the spec says to me), so I think we should refrain from speccing it to that effect (must say I kind of like the idea, though), although it's probably a corner-case (who uses that large borders, anyway?).

>  I seem to recall @MatsPalmgren having some changes in mind for the Firefox behavior in this regard? 

Right, I filed https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1485646 but I'm not sure I want to change it anymore.  We use the content-box size of the "anonymous fieldset content box":
https://whatpr.org/html/3934/rendering.html#the-fieldset-and-legend-elements:'block-size'
as the percentage basis for children other than the rendered legend. It means that 100% fills the space that's leftover after the rendered legend has taken its size and thus doesn't overflow the anon box.  It means that the rendered legend "has priority" to the available space though and that it can eagerly take all of it.  That is, for a fieldset with a content-box height of 100px we flow the rendered legend in a CB that is 100px.  Then we calculate how much remaining content-box size there is after placing it at the fieldset border-box edge. Then we set the inner anonymous border-box size to that remaining size. Then we flow the children inside the anon box content-box using that as the percentage basis. So I kinda think this makes sense to me now. As Boris points out, if we instead use the specified fieldset height as percentage basis then 100% would overflow the anon box.
If we use the box model as illustrated in that figure then I think it's the correct way to resolve percentages (per css-sizing) since the anon box is the CB for those children.
